Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma, the combination of threat items is not fully coherent: startle response and physical reactivity fit PTSD, but risky behavior is a different symptom style and is weakly connected to the rest of this profile. With only Threat and Memory represented, risky behavior lacks support from the other selected items and does not read as a clear trauma-linked threat perception.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: Within Memory, the items suggest overwhelmed, poorly verbalized traumatic recall, which is coherent for PTSD. However, intense guilt on recall introduces a strong negative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent from the profile. Given the formulation only shows a Threat → Memory link and no active Negative Appraisals connections, this item is not well aligned with the stated cognitive pattern.

vignette:
Amadou had been working late at his desk in the curriculum office when the police came to the apartment building next door. What began as the ordinary sounds of a summer night in his neighborhood in Atlanta changed in an instant: shouting in the hallway, a heavy pounding at the wrong door, radios crackling, and then the sudden crack of commands that sounded close enough to be in his own room. He froze while his wife called his name from the kitchen, and when he finally stepped into the hall he saw officers with hands on their weapons, their flashlights sweeping across the landing as if everyone there were a suspect. He was pushed back, asked where he had been, told to keep his hands visible. Nothing about his own conduct mattered in that moment; what stayed with him was the helplessness of being treated as dangerous without warning. Afterward, whenever a siren rose outside their building or he heard sharp knocking in the hallway, his body reacted before his mind could catch up. He would jerk in his chair, feel his chest tighten, and scan the room or the street with an alertness that left him exhausted by the end of the day. At work, where he designed lesson plans in a quiet office and often reviewed materials late into the evening, even a coworker appearing silently at his cubicle could make him flinch hard enough to spill coffee across his papers.

Over the following months, Amadou became increasingly watchful in ways that seemed reasonable to him, almost necessary. He checked who was outside before opening the apartment door, listened for footsteps in the stairwell, and sat with his back to the wall in restaurants. He had come to believe that danger could arrive without pattern, and that if he relaxed even briefly he might be caught off guard again. That constant alertness fed into the way the memory returned. When the recollection surfaced, it did not come to him as a full story he could tell from beginning to end. More often it arrived as a wave of unease in his chest, a hot surge of dread with no clear picture attached, and he would have to stop whatever he was doing. If his wife asked what he was thinking about, he would shake his head because he could not seem to put the event into words. He knew it happened, and he knew what it felt like, but the harder he tried to explain it, the more the details slipped away. At times the emotional force came first, arriving without an image at all, as though his body remembered what his mind could not organize.

That combination made him even more guarded. In the classroom design office, the ring of the phone or the abrupt scrape of a chair would send a jolt through him, and he would look up immediately, certain something bad was about to happen. He stopped taking the train home after dark because every uniformed figure on the platform seemed to sharpen the old fear. The less he spoke about the incident, the more it seemed to inhabit him in fragments, appearing as a rush of feeling or a bodily startle rather than a narrative. When he tried to recount what happened to his wife, he could get only as far as “they had me against the wall,” and then he would go silent, overwhelmed by the force of what came back. She noticed that he was sleeping lightly, rising at every sound from the street, and that he had grown irritable and tired, but he mostly explained it as staying careful. Careful, for Amadou, meant being superalert, scanning the room in his office, at home, and even while driving past flashing lights on the highway.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had narrowed his life. He was avoiding evening errands, lingering too long at the office to avoid crowded transit, and no longer felt fully present with his wife when they were out together. What finally brought him in was a night when an ambulance passed their building and he had such a strong physical reaction that he had to sit on the floor, breathing hard, unable to speak for several minutes. He was frightened by how quickly his body took over and by how often he was now living in anticipation of the next jolt. More than anything, Amadou hoped to stop feeling as if he had to watch every corner of every room, and he feared that if this continued he would become a stranger to his own home and to the work he had built his life around.
